lead: There is no single process called welding. There are three families, and every one ends the same way: two metal surfaces become one continuous mass at the atomic level. Either the parent metal melts, or it stays solid and is pressed and heated into contact, or only a lower-melting filler melts. Once you can place any process in its family, the rest of welding — flames, arcs, electrodes, defects — files away neatly. This classification is used every day to choose a process for a car body, a radiator, a PCB or a pipeline.
prereq: You need only that every metal has a fixed melting point. The freezing of a melt is covered in Unit 1, Metal Casting Processes.

blocks.text: Two metal surfaces touch only at a few high spots. Atoms elsewhere are too far apart to bond. Joining closes that gap until the surfaces become one continuous mass at the atomic scale. This closing is called coalescence. Every joining process is one route to coalescence.

Fusion welding melts the parent metal at the joint. The melted pool is the fusion zone; it mixes with any filler and freezes into one piece with the parent on both sides. SMAW, gas welding, laser welding and resistance spot welding all work this way.

Solid-state welding melts nothing. The surfaces are cleaned, pressed together and held below melting. Pressure breaks the oxide and flattens the high spots, and atoms diffuse across the interface with time. Friction, friction stir, ultrasonic, explosive and diffusion bonding are solid-state. No melt means no cast structure in the joint and little distortion.

The third family melts only the filler. A filler with a lower melting point melts, wets the solid parent surfaces and freezes. The parent keeps its grain structure, its heat treatment and its flatness. Brazing uses a filler melting above 450 °C; soldering uses one melting below 450 °C.

Filler words. An autogenous joint uses no filler: the parent alone closes the gap, as in spot and friction stir welding. A homogeneous joint uses filler of the same composition as the parent; a heterogeneous joint uses a different filler, such as a silver alloy joining a carbide tip to a steel shank.
T_filler < T_parent; brazing if T_filler > 450 °C, soldering if T_filler < 450 °C
blocks.where: T_filler is the melting temperature of the filler metal and T_parent that of the parts being joined, both in °C. The 450 °C line is a convention about the filler only, not a process temperature.

blocks.text: The family says what melts; the energy source says what melts it. Name both and the process is pinned down.
Gas cutting is thermal cutting, not joining; it is covered in 4.2.

Resistance spot welding is fusion for a reason. Current meets its highest resistance at the contact between the sheets, so a small lens-shaped nugget of parent metal melts there and freezes while the rest stays solid. That is why a spot-welded car body shows round marks in a row, not a continuous seam.
The flame is treated in 4.2, the arc in 4.3, arc processes in 4.4, resistance in 4.5, solid state in 4.6, laser in 4.7 and brazing in 4.8.

sections.h3: Joints, welds and choosing a process

blocks.text: A joint is the shape of the assembly. Butt: two plates in line, edge to edge. Lap: one plate lies on the other. T-joint: one plate stands on the face of another. Corner: two plates meet at a corner. Edge: two plate edges stand side by side.

A weld is the metal formed. A groove weld fills a prepared bevel between plates and is the usual weld in a butt joint. A fillet weld is triangular and sits in the corner of a lap or T-joint. A plug weld fills a hole in the top plate to reach the plate below. A spot weld is one small nugget; a seam weld is a line of overlapping spots made by rolling electrodes.

items: Thickness: thin sheet favours soldering, laser, TIG or spot; thick plate favours multi-pass arc welding into a groove.
Metal: aluminium needs AC TIG or MIG; copper and dissimilar pairs are easiest brazed.
Position: overhead and vertical work is hard for a large molten pool; low-heat processes help.
Distortion: shrinkage on freezing pulls the plate; solid-state and laser put in little heat.

blocks.text: Whatever the process, it must control heat, cleanliness and air. When one of the three is wrong, a defect appears — see 4.9.

figure.caption: Joining processes: two welding families (fusion, solid state), the filler-melting family shown as its two halves (brazing above 450 °C, soldering below), and adhesive bonding as a non-metal route outside the three.

spec.aria: A tree with root Joining branching into Fusion, Solid state, Brazing, Soldering and Adhesive, each with a note listing its example processes.

examples.question: Classify each of these five joints and state, for each, whether the parent metal melts and whether a filler is used: (a) shielded metal arc welding of a mild steel butt joint; (b) friction stir welding of 6 mm aluminium plates; (c) brazing a carbide tip to a steel shank with a silver alloy that melts at 700 °C; (d) resistance spot welding of two 1 mm car-body sheets; (e) soldering a PCB joint with Sn-63Pb, which melts at 183 °C. Second part: a copper-to-brass radiator joint must run at 300 °C. Is solder acceptable, and what would you use instead?
steps: (a) The arc melts the plate edges, so this is fusion. The consumable electrode is matching steel filler, so the joint is homogeneous. Parent melts: yes. Filler: yes.
(b) 6 mm is plate thickness, not a temperature. The rotating tool stirs the metal below melting, so this is solid state. Parent melts: no. Filler: none, so autogenous.
(c) 700 °C is above 450 °C, so this is brazing. Carbide and steel stay solid; only the silver alloy melts and wets both. Parent melts: no. Filler: yes, and heterogeneous.
(d) Current through the sheet contact melts a small nugget, so this is fusion. Parent melts: yes, only inside the nugget. Filler: none, so autogenous. The 1 mm is sheet thickness.
(e) 183 °C is below 450 °C, so this is soldering. Copper pad and component lead stay solid. Parent melts: no. Filler: yes, heterogeneous.
Second part: at 300 °C service the 183 °C filler is 117 °C below its melting point. It softens and remelts, so solder is not acceptable.

Copper melts at 1085 °C. The replacement filler must melt above 450 °C to be a brazing alloy — at least 150 °C above the 300 °C service temperature — and below copper's 1085 °C. A silver-based alloy melting near 700 °C is typical.
examples.answer: Solder melting at 183 °C sits 117 °C below the 300 °C service temperature and would soften and remelt. Braze instead with a filler melting above 450 °C and below copper's 1085 °C; a silver-based alloy near 700 °C is typical.
examples.check:
t_solder = 183
t_service = 300
shortfall = t_service - t_solder
t_copper = 1085
print(t_solder)
print(t_service)
print(shortfall)
print(t_copper)

traps: Calling brazing and soldering 'welding'. The parent never melts, so the joint is filler-held and not a fusion joint; writing 'brazing is a type of welding' loses the mark.
Calling resistance spot welding solid-state because a press closes on the sheets. The press only supplies force; the current melts a nugget, so it is fusion.
Mixing up the heat-affected zone with the fusion zone. The HAZ never melted; it only got hot enough for its structure to change.
Reading 450 °C as a process temperature. It is a line drawn on the filler's melting point alone.
Thinking autogenous means without heat. It means without filler.

quiz.q: Define coalescence and name the three families of joining processes.
quiz.a: Coalescence is two surfaces becoming one continuous mass at the atomic scale. The families are fusion, solid state, and filler-only joining (brazing and soldering).

quiz.q: At what filler melting temperature does soldering stop and brazing begin?
quiz.a: 450 °C. Below it the process is soldering, above it brazing.

quiz.q: Why does a brazed joint keep the parent metal's heat treatment while a fusion weld does not?
quiz.a: In brazing the parent never melts and stays well below its own melting point, so its grains and heat treatment survive. A fusion weld melts the parent, and the fusion zone freezes as a cast structure beside an altered heat-affected zone.

quiz.q: Distinguish the fusion zone from the heat-affected zone.
quiz.a: The fusion zone melted and then froze. The heat-affected zone never melted, but its structure and properties changed because heat reached it.

quiz.q: A filler melting at 620 °C joins two steel plates that melt near 1500 °C. Name the family, say whether the parent melts, and say whether the joint is homogeneous or heterogeneous.
quiz.a: 620 °C is above 450 °C, so it is brazing. The steel parent does not melt. The filler differs from the parent, so the joint is heterogeneous.

quiz.q: A 0.4 mm copper foil must be joined to a brass terminal with no melting of the foil and no flame. Name two families you could use and one process from each.
quiz.a: Soldering (filler melting below 450 °C) and solid-state ultrasonic welding. Both keep the foil solid; resistance spot welding would melt it and is fusion.

quiz.q: Friction stir welding joins copper to aluminium with no filler. One engineer calls the joint heterogeneous, another says the word does not apply. Explain.
quiz.a: Homogeneous and heterogeneous describe the filler against the parent. With no filler the joint is autogenous, so the labels do not apply; the joint simply joins two dissimilar metals without melting either.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry runs hybrid processes — laser-arc, friction stir with added filler, cold metal transfer — that sit between the families, so this tree is a teaching tool, not a law. Adhesive bonding is standard in aircraft and in electric-vehicle battery packs.
